facts.statement: PersonaTrail evaluates personalized web agents by analyzing browsing trails to infer user preferences and recall information.
TokenMinds introduces a new way to model user behavior in large recommender systems by capturing language semantics rather than sequential patterns in user behaviors.
TokenMinds leverages a dual-output design with a dense user embedding and discrete SID tokens to improve user understanding and performance.

sources.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
sources.description:
arXiv:2610.36435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. Specifically, negotiation parties with a user obtain higher payouts (+13.7% on average) and their agents negotiate more aggressively. Surprisingly, user presence also induces misaligned behavior, both toward counterparties (where its rate roughly doubles) and toward users (where it emerges in 14.3% of games). These misaligned behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes and persist even when the user sends only templated, neutral messages. These findings expose two blind spots in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect them.

sources.title: Cross-User Poisoning: User-Task Boundary Failures in Multi-User Collaborative Language Agents
sources.description:
arXiv:2511.17671v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Language agents are moving from single-user assistants to shared collaborators in workspaces, forums, and group chats. A shared agent observes interleaved messages from multiple users, maintains persistent context, and executes tool actions, creating a boundary problem absent from standard single-user agents: the agent must decide not only whether an instruction is safe, but which user or task it is allowed to govern. We identify cross-user poisoning (CUP), where an adversary injects a message into shared context that is later applied while the agent serves a benign user, causing unauthorized actions or responses outside the instruction's intended scope. We validate CUP on two deployed multi-user agents, Continua and ElizaOS, and introduce MURMUR, a framework for evaluating shared-context agents under concurrent multi-user interactions. Across Slack, Workspace, and Airline domains, CUP achieves high attack success, persists across later interactions, and remains substantially more effective than matched prompt-injection attacks. We evaluate boundary-scoping defenses and find that context summarization alone is insufficient, while task clustering and provenance prompting substantially reduce non-adaptive propagation. These results show that robust multi-user agents require explicit user/task scoping rather than generic input filtering or context compression.

sources.title: TokenMinds: Pretrained User Tokens and Embeddings for User Understanding in Large Recommender Systems
sources.description:
arXiv:2606.25147v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: User modeling in industrial recommender systems typically produces dense embeddings, which suffer from representational constraints due to fixed-dimensional vectors. As an emerging alternative for discrete user representation, LLM-generated natural-language user profiles often capture language semantics rather than sequential patterns in user behaviors. Meanwhile, Semantic ID (SID) is effective for item representation, yet existing discrete user representations remain largely confined to quantizing already-pooled user vectors, clustering historical watches, or predicting coarse topic clusters solely for candidate retrieval. We propose TokenMinds, an industrial system that extends the PLUM framework from SID-based item retrieval to generative sequential user modeling. Built on an encoder-decoder architecture adapted from pretrained LLMs, TokenMinds introduces a dual-output design: the encoder outputs a dense user embedding capturing a holistic user state, while the decoder generates discrete SID-based user tokens representing multi-faceted future interests. Grounded in item semantics, these tokens preserve distinct interests that a single pooled vector would average away. Additionally, a shared SID vocabulary across long- and short-form videos unifies cross-scenario behaviors into a single model, cutting upstream training and serving compute by 50% and 31%. Furthermore, leveraging the text vocabulary inherited from the pretrained LLM, TokenMinds interleaves textual search queries directly with watch histories to capture explicit user intent. We validate TokenMinds through offline evaluations and live A/B experiments across YouTube's primary ranking surfaces, serving billions of users asynchronously: SID-based user tokens are effective on their own, yield additive gains alongside dense embeddings, and together outperform the previous-generation, non-LLM user model in production.
